body:
I would keep the public hook small, but make the thing passed through it an explicit proposed-call envelope rather than loose tool name plus args. That gives policy code a stable object to decide on without forcing LangGraph to standardize every downstream governance system.

The envelope I would want before execution is:

- `tool_call_id` and attempt id

- tool name plus canonicalized args digest, with redaction rules for raw args

- graph/run/thread identifiers when available

- state digest or selected state refs, not necessarily the full state object

- tool classification: read-only, external write, credentialed, network, filesystem, payment, etc.

- resume/retry context: first attempt, replay, resumed interrupt, or retry after failure

- policy profile/version from config

Then the hook can still return a simple decision: allow, block, modify, or interrupt for approval. The important invariant is that the decision is bound to the proposed envelope, and execution must re-check that the envelope did not mutate before the tool actually runs.

The tests I would add are the cases that tend to break production agents: block happens before any side effect; modified args produce a new digest and decision; an approval interrupt resumes only the same envelope; a retry either consumes a retryable decision or forces revalidation; and a tool exception still emits a terminal outcome record linked back to the decision. Those tests make the hook useful as an operations boundary, not just a callback convenience.

Disclosure: I work on Armorer Labs.

body:
Yes, that is the invariant I would make explicit: a policy verdict is only executable if it binds to the effective envelope at the final pre-call gate. The proposed envelope is useful for interruption and review, but it should not be the authorization object once any modify step has happened.

I would model this as three separate references rather than one overloaded id:

- `proposed_call_id`: stable handle for the model-requested call and any human review UI
- `decision_ref`: the allow/block/modify decision, including the envelope digest it evaluated
- `effective_call_id` plus `effective_digest`: the exact call about to execute after modification, canonicalization, default injection, or resume

Then the gate rule is boring and testable: execute only when the terminal allow decision is bound to `effective_digest`; fail closed when the decision is absent, expired, scoped to another policy profile, or signed over a different digest. I agree mismatched evidence should be its own terminal outcome, not collapsed into missing approval, because it tells operators whether they had an auth outage or an integrity mismatch.

The other place this matters is retry/resume. A resumed interrupt should not reuse a proposed-call approval if the effective args are reconstructed differently, even if the visible tool name and call id look unchanged. Recompute the effective digest at the final boundary, compare it to the decision binding, and emit the mismatch as a first-class outcome record.

body:
Issue:
`_generate_ms_seq_id()` hardcodes the sequence to `0`, meaning events fired in the same
millisecond share the same ID — and during reconnect, the `Last-Event-ID` comparison silently drops the second one, causing lost stream frames.

My proposed fix is to track the last emitted millisecond and increment a sequence counter per-collision, wrapped in a `threading.Lock()` for safety — so IDs go `<ms>-0`, `<ms>-1`, `<ms>-2` instead of all being `<ms>-0`. The reporter has already sketched this approach in the issue description, so the main work is implementing, testing, and landing it.

Please assign this issue to me.. Gonna ensure nothing breaks and add regression testing as well..
author: bisma-nawaz

body:
> 问题： `_generate_ms_seq_id()`将序列硬编码为`0`，这意味着在同一时间触发的事件 毫秒共享同一个 ID——在重新连接期间，`Last-Event-ID`比较时会悄悄丢弃第二个，导致丢失流帧。
> 
> 我提出的解决方案是跟踪最后发出的毫秒数，并在每次碰撞时递增一个序列计数器，`threading.Lock()`为了安全起见，将其封装在一个 `<std::string>` 中——这样 ID 就会变成 `<std:: string>` `<ms>-0`、 `<std::string>``<ms>-1`而`<ms>-2`不是全部都是 `<std:: `<ms>-0`string>`。报告者已经在问题描述中概述了这种方法，因此主要工作是实现、测试和最终确定该方案。
> 
> 请把这个问题分配给我。我会确保一切正常，并添加回归测试。

Thanks so much for offering to take this on — really appreciate it! 🙏 Since I'd already been digging around in inmem_stream.py, let me share a few things I ran into that might save you some time while you implement it.

The replay comparison probably needs to change alongside the ID generation. restore_messages filters with message.id.decode() > message_id, which is a lexicographic string compare. That's fine for -0 through -9, but once the sequence hits double digits it flips: "…132-2" > "…132-10" is True. So with a per-millisecond counter in place, a reconnect at Last-Event-ID=…-10 would re-emit seq 2–9 as duplicates rather than skipping them. And since a lot of token deltas can land in the same millisecond, seq ≥ 10 is realistically the common case — which is exactly when the counter kicks in. Two clean ways around it: zero-pad the sequence to a fixed width, or split ms-seq into an (int(ms), int(seq)) tuple for the comparison. Just wanted to flag it so the fix doesn't accidentally trade dropped frames for duplicated ones.

Minor note on the lock: since put/put_thread are async def on a single asyncio loop and there's no await between reading the clock and bumping the counter, that section is already atomic with respect to the loop — so a threading.Lock may not be needed here (though happy to be corrected if there's a cross-thread path I'm missing).

One robustness thought for later: time.time() isn't monotonic, so a clock adjustment could move ms backwards and sort a new event before an older one. Tracking last_ms = max(last_ms, now) would cover that, if you want to fold it in.

A regression test that fires >10 events within a single millisecond, disconnects mid-stream, and asserts exactly-once replay would nail down both the counter and the comparison edge. Glad to review whenever you open a PR — thanks again for picking it up!

body:
Reproduced your TOCTOU. The barrier-synced repro nails it: every thread reads the same `checkpoint_pending_writes` snapshot, filters out its own `task_id`, then reassigns the list wholesale before extending, so the last assignment silently drops every other thread's pending writes. The 30/30 determinism is the tell that it's structural, not a flake.

Your fix in #8114 (`_pending_writes_lock` around the read-filter-assign-extend) is the right narrow fix. If a maintainer ever pushes back on a lock in that path, the unsafe part is specifically the rebind. `self.checkpoint_pending_writes = [...]` swaps the list out from under concurrent readers, so an in-place mutation that never reassigns the attribute would also close it, though the single guarded section you wrote is the simplest. Might also be worth scanning the other `BackgroundExecutor`-driven mutations on shared loop state for the same read-then-rebind shape.

The reason it's stuck looks like process, not code. The `require-issue-link` bot auto-closed #8114 about a minute after you opened it, because external contributors have to be assigned to the linked issue first. Opening #8115 was the right move. The missing step is a maintainer assigning you to it, after which #8114 can be reopened. That bot catches a lot of external fix PRs here.

If the fix serializes `aput` operations on a single connection, the test should still run many concurrent tasks so it proves callers can keep the same public concurrency pattern without surfacing `database is locked`. author: hiSandog

body:
Took a look at the source — I think the issue's repro and the proposed `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` fix don't quite line up, and there's a smaller intervention that's more likely to address the production failure mode.

**The `asyncio.Lock` already serializes within one saver.** `aput` (`libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/aio.py:537`) and `aput_writes` (line 584) both wrap the `execute` + `commit` in `async with self.lock:`. The setup at line 312 also holds the lock. The 50-worker repro uses a single `AsyncSqliteSaver` instance with `:memory:`, which means all 50 coroutines funnel through one `asyncio.Lock` and one underlying `aiosqlite` connection — the workers cannot execute concurrently at the SQLite level. If you can actually reproduce `database is locked` with the snippet as written, that's a different bug class (e.g., aiosqlite queuing the next statement on its worker thread before the previous `commit` resolves) and worth a stack trace.

**The real failure mode is cross-connection, not within-saver.** `"database is locked"` from SQLite is raised when a different OS-level connection holds the write lock. That happens when:

- Multiple `AsyncSqliteSaver` instances open the same on-disk file (e.g., one per process, or two savers in one process),
- Or `SqliteSaver` (sync) and `AsyncSqliteSaver` are pointed at the same file.

`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` (line 318) helps — readers don't block writers and vice-versa — but writers still serialize, and **`busy_timeout` defaults to 0**, so the *first* contended write raises immediately instead of waiting. There's no `busy_timeout` set anywhere in `checkpoint-sqlite` today.

**Proposed fix (smallest correct shape):**

```python
# libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/aio.py:318, inside setup()
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;
PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000;   -- 5s: retry on SQLITE_BUSY before raising
```

This is the SQLite-recommended knob for exactly this symptom. Five seconds is a common default (matches e.g. aiosqlite's own docs); the value is configurable if a maintainer wants it tunable. The same PRAGMA should land in the sync `SqliteSaver.setup` for parity.

**Why not `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`:**

- The current code uses `self.conn.execute(...)` + `await self.conn.commit()` and relies on the DB-API implicit transaction. There's no explicit `BEGIN` anywhere in `aio.py`. Switching to `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` requires restructuring every `aput`/`aput_writes`/`adelete_thread` into explicit-transaction form (you can't `executescript` a `BEGIN` in py3 sqlite3, and you can't `BEGIN` while inside an open transaction — it gets fiddly).
- `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` acquires the write lock at `BEGIN` time, which serializes the whole transaction including any read preamble. For the single-connection saver that's strictly worse than what the `asyncio.Lock` already does.
- `busy_timeout` addresses the actual cross-connection case without restructuring transaction handling.

**Test plan I'd include in a PR:**

1. Open two `AsyncSqliteSaver` instances against the same on-disk temp file.
2. Fire N concurrent `aput` calls across both savers.
3. Without the fix: surface `OperationalError: database is locked` reliably within a few iterations.
4. With `busy_timeout=5000`: same scenario completes cleanly.

I cannot reproduce the bug with the issue's single-saver `:memory:` snippet, so a maintainer should confirm whether multi-connection contention is the intended target before merging — but `busy_timeout` is cheap and correct to set regardless of that answer, since it has no downside for the within-saver case.

Happy to open the PR if this shape looks right.
author: ly-wang19

body:
### Test Coverage & Documentation Considerations

To ensure this is robust moving forward, the regression test should ideally cover two main aspects:

1. **The Multi-Connection Race:** As outlined above, testing with multiple separate saver instances hitting the same file to ensure `busy_timeout` handles the contention cleanly.
2. **The Async Fan-Out (Public API Safety):** Even though the internal `asyncio.Lock` serializes execution within a single connection, the test should still fire a massive fan-out of concurrent tasks (just like the original reproduction snippet). This guarantees that from the caller's perspective, the public concurrency pattern remains completely safe and doesn't leak any underlying `database is locked` operational errors.

#### Note on Scope & Documentation
Given that SQLite is generally optimized for local development or lightweight single-process applications, it might also be worth adding a small note to the LangGraph documentation. Clarifying whether `SqliteSaver` / `AsyncSqliteSaver` are officially intended for highly concurrent, multi-process production environments—or if production workloads with high concurrency should strictly point towards more robust production checkpointers (like Postgres)—would be incredibly helpful for architectural decisions.

Let me know if this comprehensive approach makes sense, and I can include both the fix and the updated test suite in the PR!

body:
The split between live context and persistent memory is the part I’d make very explicit for LangGraph users.

They solve different problems:

```text
live context        = what is true before this run starts
checkpoint state    = where this graph execution currently is
persistent memory   = what should survive across runs/sessions/projects
```

A middleware/checkpointer integration should probably avoid collapsing those into one abstraction. Service health, workspace config, recent activity, and project memory have different freshness and authority rules.

For example, a retrieved persistent memory should carry metadata like:

```text
memory_type: decision | failed_path | convention | preference | open_question
scope: user | project | workspace
source_ref
last_confirmed_at
status: candidate | accepted | superseded
```

Then a LangGraph app can decide whether the memory is prior context, a constraint, or only a hypothesis.

I’ve been working around a similar Personal AI OS / Memory Vault pattern: authored/project memory should be durable and inspectable, while generated recall/context views remain rebuildable runtime layers.

Refs:
- https://github.com/hegu-1/personal-memory-vault-starter
- https://github.com/hegu-1/personal-ai-os

body:
I'd like to work on this, and I want to align on the approach before opening a PR.

Root cause: `_msgpack_default` in `jsonplus.py` special-cases `set`/`frozenset`/`deque`, but `dict` subclasses are serialized via `ormsgpack`'s native map path and never reach it, so they decode as a plain `dict` (dropping `default_factory` for `defaultdict`, and the type/semantics of `Counter`/`OrderedDict`).

The cleanest interception point I've found is enabling `ormsgpack.OPT_PASSTHROUGH_SUBCLASS` and adding explicit handlers for `defaultdict`/`Counter`/`OrderedDict`. The one tradeoff to flag: that option also routes other native-base subclasses (e.g. numpy scalars such as `np.int64`) through `default`, so to avoid regressions I'd add a fallback that encodes any unhandled subclass as its base type, with round-trip tests across `str`/`int`/`list`/`dict` subclasses and numpy scalars. Pre-fix checkpoints would still load unchanged.

Does that approach align with what you'd want — and should `Counter`/`OrderedDict` be preserved too, or just `defaultdict`? If it sounds good, could a maintainer assign me and I'll open the PR.
author: OmkumarSolanki

body:
Confirmed the silent downcast on current `main` for all three subclasses (`defaultdict(list)`, `Counter`, `OrderedDict`) via the reproduction in the issue body. `type(restored).__name__` comes back as `dict` for each, and `defaultdict`'s `default_factory` / `Counter.most_common` / `OrderedDict.move_to_end` are all lost.

## Where it happens

The encoder fallback at `libs/checkpoint/langgraph/checkpoint/serde/jsonplus.py:_msgpack_default` only special-cases `set`, `frozenset`, and `deque` from `collections` — everything else that subclasses `dict` falls through to ormsgpack's built-in dict encoding, which discards the subclass. The decoder then reconstructs a plain `dict` because the type tag was never recorded.

This is the same shape as #8157 (deque `maxlen` lost) — a subclass with constructor state beyond the items isn't round-tripping.

## Proposed encoding per subclass

Mapping each to the existing ExtType codes (so no protocol/format change):

| Subclass | ExtType | Reconstruct shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Counter` | `EXT_CONSTRUCTOR_SINGLE_ARG` | `Counter(dict(items))` — Counter's `__init__` accepts a dict, count semantics preserved |
| `OrderedDict` | `EXT_CONSTRUCTOR_POS_ARGS` | `OrderedDict([(k, v), ...])` — preserves order explicitly even though `dict` is ordered in 3.7+ |
| `defaultdict` | `EXT_CONSTRUCTOR_KW_ARGS` | `defaultdict(default_factory=..., items_dict)` — but see below |

`Counter` and `OrderedDict` are clean wins: single-arg / list-of-pairs constructors, no extra state.

`defaultdict`'s `default_factory` is the awkward one. It can be:
- a builtin (`list`, `int`, `set`) — encodable as `(module, name)` and reconstructed via import
- `None` (default_factory is optional) — trivially encodable
- a lambda / custom callable — not safely encodable without pickle fallback

The first two cover the overwhelmingly common case. The third is the same pickle-fallback escape hatch langgraph already uses elsewhere, or it could be a "warn and drop to plain dict" degradation (matching how `_warn_once` handles unregistered types at `jsonplus.py:73`).

## Backwards compatibility

Old checkpoints written before this fix deserialize as plain `dict` (same as today), so the change is purely additive on the encode side — there's no migration debt and no risk of breaking existing sessions. Worth gating the new branches behind `isinstance(obj, defaultdict)` etc. so a user subclassing `dict` for their own purposes still gets the existing plain-dict behavior unless they explicitly opt into one of the three stdlib subclasses.

## Notes

- The `external` label and the closed-but-unfixed state of #8157 suggest langgraph gates external-contributor PRs behind an explicit assign step before a PR can land. I'm not asking for assignment in this comment — just sharing the analysis. Happy to defer to a maintainer's preferred encoding shape if the above isn't what they want.

body:
Hi 👋 I'd like to work on this if it's still available.

I confirmed the bug and want to share one finding that shapes the fix: the `try/except RuntimeError: pass` block isn't purely a mistake — it's there to swallow `RuntimeError("no running event loop")` from `asyncio.current_task()` when `get_config` is called from a **sync** context. I verified empirically that `asyncio.current_task()` raises that error outside an event loop on **both** 3.10 and 3.11+, so simply removing the `try/except` would leak "no running event loop" to sync callers instead of the intended "Called get_config outside of a runnable context".

The actual bug is that the guard's own `raise RuntimeError("Python 3.11 or later required...")` lives **inside** that same `try`, so the broad handler catches and discards it.

Proposed fix: catch the `current_task()` call separately to detect whether we're in an async context, then raise the guard **outside** that handler:
```python
try:
    in_async_context = asyncio.current_task() is not None
except RuntimeError:
    in_async_context = False
if in_async_context:
    raise RuntimeError("Python 3.11 or later required to use this in an async context")
```
Sync behavior is unchanged; the guard now propagates correctly on Python < 3.11.

I have the fix ready on a branch off `main`, with tests that monkeypatch `sys.version_info` to force the `< 3.11` branch (since CI runs on 3.11+) and assert the guard fires inside an async task, does not fire in a sync context, and that its message is distinct from the event-loop error.

If assigned I'll open the PR. Could you assign this to me?

body:
Confirmed the bug on current `main` (`libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/chat_agent_executor.py:621-632`), but the repro in the issue body needs a small tweak: passing `remaining_steps: 1` in the **input dict** does not actually flow into the abort check, because `remaining_steps` in the agent state is the `RemainingSteps` managed value derived from `recursion_limit - step`. Setting it on the input gets overwritten by the reducer on the very first step. With the issue's literal repro, the abort check sees `remaining_steps = recursion_limit - 1` (default `recursion_limit = 25`), so the second branch never fires and the tool returns correctly.

To trigger the actual defect, set a low `recursion_limit` in the config so `remaining_steps` legitimately reaches 1 at the model node:

```python
result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [HumanMessage("run tool")]},
    config={"recursion_limit": 2},
)
# Actual:   "Sorry, need more steps to process this request."
# Expected: "direct answer"
```

## Root cause

`_are_more_steps_needed` returns `True` (abort) when `remaining_steps < 2 and has_tool_calls`, regardless of whether the pending tool calls are `return_direct`:

```python
if remaining_steps is not None:
    if remaining_steps < 1 and all_tools_return_direct:
        return True
    elif remaining_steps < 2 and has_tool_calls:   # ← fires even when all tools are return_direct
        return True
```

With `remaining_steps == 1` and a `return_direct=True` tool call, the first branch is `False` (1 is not < 1) and the second branch is `True` (`1 < 2 and has_tool_calls`), so the run aborts even though a `return_direct` tool needs no second LLM turn — the ToolNode output goes straight to the user via the early-exit at `chat_agent_executor.py:~985`.

The intent of the first branch (`remaining_steps < 1 and all_tools_return_direct`) only makes sense if `return_direct` tools are also exempted from the second branch; otherwise that first branch is unreachable through normal flow.

## Minimal fix

```python
elif remaining_steps < 2 and has_tool_calls and not all_tools_return_direct:
    return True
```

This preserves the abort for the normal case (non-`return_direct` tools genuinely need a follow-up model turn), while letting a final step proceed when every pending tool call is `return_direct` and therefore cannot trigger another model invocation.

## Test coverage

The existing `test_return_direct` in `libs/prebuilt/tests/test_react_agent.py` only exercises the default-`recursion_limit` path. A regression test for this fix would invoke the agent with `config={"recursion_limit": 2}` and a single `return_direct=True` tool call, asserting the tool message (not the "need more steps" sentinel) is the final message.

I'm happy to open a PR with the one-line fix + regression test if a maintainer confirms the diagnosis.

body:
Hi 👋 I'd like to work on this if it's still available.

I dug into the root cause and want to flag one nuance the report (and the prior closed PRs) gloss over: `remaining_steps` isn't read from the input state — `RemainingStepsManager` recomputes it as `recursion_limit − current_step`, so the actual trigger is `recursion_limit=2`, not a user-supplied `remaining_steps: 1`.

The current `_are_more_steps_needed` has two problems:
1. `remaining_steps < 2 and has_tool_calls` aborts **any** tool call, including terminal `return_direct` tools → the silent "Sorry, need more steps" AIMessage.
2. The sibling `remaining_steps < 1 and all_tools_return_direct` branch is inverted — 0 steps left is fatal regardless of whether the pending tools are terminal.

Proposed fix: make `< 1` unconditionally fatal, and gate the `< 2` abort on `not all_tools_return_direct` so terminal tools are allowed through.

One caveat I verified empirically: a single-turn `return_direct` call structurally needs 3 Pregel supersteps (agent → tools → route resolution), so `recursion_limit=2` still can't complete it — but after the fix it surfaces a `GraphRecursionError` instead of silently aborting, and it completes normally at `recursion_limit=3`. So this fix removes the spurious abort and the inverted branch; making `rl=2` itself succeed would be a separate (engine-level) change. Happy to scope that if you'd like, but I think the logic fix here is the right first step.

I have the fix + a regression test ready on a branch off `main`. If assigned I'll open the PR. Could you assign this to me?

body:
This is a control-flow preservation boundary issue.

The key distinction is:

  middleware-wrapped tool execution
  !=
  permission to downgrade graph control-flow into tool error output

From the issue, the direct path preserves the interrupt correctly:

  tool calls interrupt()
  → GraphInterrupt / GraphBubbleUp is raised
  → graph suspends
  → interrupt payload remains resumable

But the wrapper path changes the class of the transition:

  tool calls interrupt()
  → GraphInterrupt reaches awrap_tool_call path
  → broad except Exception catches it
  → handle_tool_errors converts it to a ToolMessage
  → graph continues as if the tool failed
  → interrupt payload is lost

So the failure is not only that an exception handler is too broad.

The failure is that a resumable control-flow signal is being reclassified as terminal tool failure when it crosses the middleware boundary.

A minimal conformance fixture could be:

case_1:
  awrap_tool_call_present: false
  tool_calls_interrupt: true
  graph_suspends: true
  interrupt_payload_preserved: true
  expected: CONFORMANT

case_2:
  awrap_tool_call_present: true
  tool_calls_interrupt: true
  GraphInterrupt_caught_by_exception_handler: true
  returned_as_tool_error: true
  graph_suspends: false
  expected: NON_CONFORMANT

case_3:
  awrap_tool_call_present: true
  exception_type: GraphBubbleUp
  wrapper_path_reraises: false
  expected: NON_CONFORMANT
  reason: graph control-flow must not be routed through tool-error handling

case_4:
  awrap_tool_call_present: true
  tool_raises_ValueError: true
  returned_as_tool_error: true
  expected: CONFORMANT
  reason: ordinary tool failures may still be handled as tool errors

case_5:
  awrap_tool_call_present: true
  tool_calls_interrupt: true
  wrapper_path_reraises_GraphBubbleUp: true
  graph_suspends: true
  interrupt_payload_preserved: true
  expected: CONFORMANT

The invariant I would preserve is:

  middleware may wrap tool execution,
  but it must not change the semantic class of graph-level control-flow.

So:

  ordinary tool exception
    → may become tool-error

  GraphInterrupt / GraphBubbleUp
    → must remain graph control-flow

Otherwise the graph has two incompatible states:

  inside the tool:
    execution requested a resumable interrupt

  after the wrapper:
    execution appears to have failed terminally

That breaks HITL, client-side delegation, and any resume protocol because the support needed for resume is flattened into an error string.

The proposed fix is the right minimal boundary repair:

  in the async wrapper path:
    except GraphBubbleUp:
      raise

  before:
    except Exception as e:
      handle_tool_errors(e)

and the same guard should exist in the sync wrapper path for symmetry.

The important point is not only “do not catch GraphInterrupt”.

It is:

  do not let wrapper middleware erase the difference between resumable graph control-flow and ordinary tool failure.

This is a transition-sufficiency issue:

  the wrapped tool transition is treated as valid,
  but the support required to preserve interrupt/resume semantics
  is not carried across the middleware execution boundary.

body:
The failure class here is a control-flow signal getting caught by a generic error boundary and silently converted into data — GraphInterrupt is being treated like any other tool exception instead of the out-of-band signal it's meant to be.

The issue itself pins the root cause precisely: "The bug is a missing `except GraphBubbleUp: raise` guard in the wrapper code path — present in the direct execution path but absent in the wrapper path." That's the whole bug in one sentence. `awrap_tool_call`'s `except Exception` block sits between the tool body and the node's own bubble-up handling, and nothing tells it that `GraphInterrupt` (a `GraphBubbleUp` subclass) is not a real failure — so it gets handed to `handle_tool_errors` and stringified into a `ToolMessage`, which is exactly what the repro shows: `"Tool call failed (GraphInterrupt): (Interrupt(value={...}),)"` instead of a suspended graph.

The deterministic check that catches this before it ships: at the boundary where any user-supplied wrapper's exception handler is invoked, assert the caught exception is not an instance of `GraphBubbleUp` before calling `handle_tool_errors` — a one-line `isinstance` guard, tested by a contract test that runs the *same* tool once with no middleware and once with a transparent pass-through middleware and diffs the two outcomes. Any wrapper/no-wrapper divergence on a `GraphInterrupt`-raising tool should fail CI. That symmetry test is cheap and would have caught this on the first PR that added `awrap_tool_call`, since the direct path already had the guard and the wrapper path didn't.

Honest uncertainty: I haven't run this against the actual `tool_node.py` source, so I can't confirm the exact line/method name of the wrapper's except block — that would need a look at the 1.2.6 source to nail down where the guard goes versus where it currently doesn't.

Full redacted write-up: https://impartshadow.github.io/echo-site/failure-cases/graphinterrupt-not-re-raised-in-awrap-tool-call-wrap-292e4a05d8.html — I triage one of these in public every day.

If this diagnosis is useful, react 👍 to this comment; if it is wrong, react 👎 — I use the verdict to choose what I investigate next.

body:
This is a control-flow classification boundary issue.

The key distinction is:

  interrupt control-flow != tool execution failure

From the issue, the runtime state is:

  tool calls interrupt()
  GraphInterrupt / GraphBubbleUp is raised
  graph should pause and preserve structured interrupt payload

But the tools stream reports:

  event: tool-error
  message: str(error)

So the interrupt changes class while crossing the stream boundary:

  structured pause signal
  → flattened error string

That loses the operational support required by any consumer that needs to resume:

  interrupt id
  interrupt value
  resumable state
  control-flow classification

The failing transition is:

  tool execution
  → interrupt raised
  → stream handler observes exception
  → stream event emitted
  → client decides whether this is pause/resume or failure

The stream handler is treating all exceptions as errors, but GraphInterrupt is not an ordinary tool exception. It is a state-transition signal.

A minimal conformance fixture could be:

case_1:
  tool_calls_interrupt: true
  exception_type: GraphInterrupt
  emitted_event: tool-error
  payload_flattened_to_string: true
  expected: NON_CONFORMANT
  reason: pause/resume control-flow was emitted as tool failure

case_2:
  tool_calls_interrupt: true
  exception_type: GraphBubbleUp
  emitted_event: tool-error
  expected: NON_CONFORMANT
  reason: GraphBubbleUp must preserve control-flow semantics across the stream boundary

case_3:
  tool_calls_interrupt: true
  structured_interrupt_payload_present: true
  emitted_as_pause_or_no_error: true
  graph_state_interrupts_contains_payload: true
  expected: CONFORMANT

case_4:
  tool_raises_value_error: true
  emitted_event: tool-error
  message_present: true
  expected: CONFORMANT
  reason: ordinary tool exceptions should still be tool errors

case_5:
  tool_calls_interrupt: true
  stream_event_contains_only_str_error: true
  client_can_recover_interrupt_id: false
  expected: NON_CONFORMANT

The invariant I would preserve is:

  a stream event must not downgrade a resumable control-flow signal into an error event.

Otherwise the framework has two incompatible states:

  graph state:
    this is a resumable interrupt

  tools stream:
    this is a tool failure string

That breaks downstream consumers because they can no longer distinguish:

  pause awaiting human input
  vs
  failed tool execution

The proposed fix in the issue looks right:

  in StreamToolCallHandler._error,
  after cleanup,
  do not emit tool-error for GraphBubbleUp / GraphInterrupt;
  let it bubble through the same control-flow path used elsewhere.

The important point is not only avoiding a misleading event name.

It is preserving the support needed for resume:

  structured interrupt id
  structured interrupt value
  resumable classification
  graph state consistency

If that support is flattened to a string, the transition cannot be safely resumed by a client.

This is a transition-sufficiency issue:

  the stream transition is treated as valid,
  but the support required to preserve pause/resume semantics
  is not carried across the tools-stream boundary.

body:
Hi @HumphreySun98, thanks for the detailed write-up and the profiling data. I'd like to take this one.

I've read through the code in `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_runner.py` and your analysis is correct — the `should_stop(self.done)` call inside `FuturesDict.on_done` re-scans every terminal future on every callback, which is pure waste since their `cancelled()`/`exception()` state is immutable.

A few observations from reading the surrounding code, which line up with your reasoning:

- `on_done` is only an early-wake path; the authoritative stop/panic decision lives in `tick`/`atick` (L330/L539) and `_panic_or_proceed` (L650), both of which still operate on the full set, so narrowing the `on_done` check to `{fut}` is safe.
- `commit` is called *inside* `on_done` before `should_stop`, so by the time we check `{fut}`, the just-completed future's exception id has already been added to `_handled_exception_ids` if it was routed to the error handler — no semantics change for graph-error-handled futures.
- The waiter future path (`value is None` in `__setitem__`) doesn't register a done callback, so it doesn't participate in this loop at all and the fix is scoped to real task futures.
- Both `tick` and `atick` inject `_should_stop_others` as `should_stop`, so a single one-line change in `on_done` covers both sync and async.

I'd like to go ahead and open the PR with `Fixes #8240` — could a maintainer assign this issue to me? Happy to run the full sync + async pregel suite (cancellation, interrupt, `max_concurrency`, retry paths) and a fan-out benchmark to back up the call-count and wall-clock numbers.
